newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Royale Belge to rely on BBL for H1 profit.
newsitem.headline: Royale Belge to rely on BBL for H1 profit.

text.p: Major Belgian insurer Groupe Royale Belge is likely to rely more on its stake in BBL bank and income from Dutch units than on internal growth when it announces a sub-12 percent first-half 1996 profit rise.
Analysts' forecasts for first half group net profit ranged from 5.0 to 5.3 billion against 4.5 billion a year earlier.
"It seems a lot at first sight, but 5.3 billion is quite modest," said Dirk Peeters at KB Securities. "Anything below 5.0 billion would not be good," he said.
Royale Belge announces H1 earnings on Wednesday.
Stephane Roffler at Mignon, Hanart et Declerck said he expected a rise of at least 12 percent -- to 5.0 billion.
"5.6 billion, 6.0 billion, it's all possible, it depends on their policy for technical reserves," said Danny Wittenberg at Dewaay, Servais & Cie.
He added Royale Belge could even show a profit of 6.5 billion if it wanted but would opt for regular growth.
"The company just wants to grow gently," he said. "It has the potential to rise by 10 percent each year."
Peeters saw H1 internal profit growth of 250 million francs, which represented a "very modest" 5.6 percent profit rise.

Analysts expected the profit rise to be fuelled mainly by the consolidation -- for the first time in half-year earnings -- of Royale Belge's 12.35 percent stake in Banque Bruxelles Lambert (BBL), which would earn it 630 million francs.

To see the earnings growth, you had to subtract from this 630 million francs around 280 million francs of net dividend income that Royale Belge would have booked using its previous method of consolidation, he noted.
"You cannot consolidate it twice," he said.
About 200 million francs in additional profit is likely to be provided by Royale Belge's Dutch operations, he added.
Royale Belge has 51 percent in holding UAP-NRB Holding NL, which fully controls insurers UAP Nederland and Nieuw Rotterdam Beheer, making it the eighth largest in the Netherlands.

Peeters said the profit contribution from the Netherlands could be higher than the estimated 200 million as non-life insurance business had been strong in the Netherlands. "But even then it will mainly be the consolidation effect," he said.
Wittenberg also said that Royale Belge's two Dutch units would account for much of the group's growth potential in the years ahead because of considerable room for synergies.
Most analysts said they recommended Royale Belge as a hold and believed its price was "fairly cheap".

But some added they would await the final impact of the re-weighting of Brussels' Bel-20 index -- which takes effect on September 23 -- before considering adjusting their advice. Royale Belge's part in the index falls to 68 shares from 100.

Royale Belge is responsible for the interests of French Union des Assurances de Paris (UAP) -- which holds a 49 percent direct and indirect stake in Royale Belge -- in the Benelux and Northern Europe.
